AuthSource.description:
Where an authorization row's value came from.

A row resolved from the project's own configuration and a row that took
the skill's default are different facts, and the record exists to stop a
decision being re-litigated mid-run.

CommandMode.description: Which of the three interpreters produced a result.

CommandOutcome.description:
What a command concluded. The exit status is derived from this rather
than chosen beside it, so the two cannot disagree.

CommandResult.description:
The whole result every swarm command emits under --full-result.

Emitted on every exit status, including a non-zero one, so a consumer
parsing the result never has to fall back to reading prose to learn
why.

command.description: The invocation path, for example "swarm manifest get".

contract_version.description:
The version of the JSON contract this result was produced against,
so a consumer branches on the version it was handed rather than on the
binary's own version.

facts.description: What the command established, in report order.

invocations.description: Every step the plan considered, in the order it considered them.

resolution.description:
What would resolve the condition. Present whenever the outcome is
attention; empty otherwise.

run.description:
The run epic this invocation was scoped to. Empty for a command
that is not run-scoped.

status.description: The exit status the outcome implies.

summary.description: One line saying what the command found. Empty when there is none.

transcript.description:
What the plan runner printed — the explained invocations in explain
mode, and the executed ones otherwise.

CountAuthRow.description: An authorization row whose resolved value is a count.

Fact.description:
One thing a command reports, with the invocations that established it.

An agent that can see the command behind a line can re-run it, argue with
it, and work around it when the underlying tool changes; an agent that
cannot has to trust a wrapper it did not write. So the invocations are
part of the fact rather than a separate section.

established.description:
Whether the value could be read at all.

A fact that could not be taken is still reported — as unestablished,
with a reason — rather than omitted or emitted as an empty value of its
type. When this is false the value is absent and the reason says why;
when it is true the value is present.

Established is not the same as satisfactory: a value that was read and
is wrong is established AND carries a reason.

invocations.description:
The commands a reader can re-run to reproduce the fact, each
with its executable first. At least one.

name.description: What the fact is. A consumer keys on this, so it is a contract.

reason.description:
What is wrong with this fact: why it could not be taken, or what is
wrong with the value it carries. Empty when nothing is.

resolution.description:
What would put THIS fact right, when anything would. Empty
otherwise.

Separate from the result's own resolution because a command reporting
several unsatisfied properties resolves each differently — naming the
key to write, not the shape of the command that writes one.

value.description: What was established. Absent when the fact was not.

FactKind.description: Which of four shapes a fact's value takes.

FactValue.description:
The value of an established fact.

A closed set of shapes rather than an open one: a consumer branches on
the kind and reads the field that kind carries, instead of guessing at
the JSON type it was handed.

Exactly one of the four value fields is present, and it is the one the
kind names. That is a rule the shape cannot state — a schema can say
which fields may appear, not which combination is coherent — so it is
enforced where the value is built, and a value carrying the wrong field
for its kind is refused rather than rendered.

count.description: Present when the kind is count.

flag.description: Present when the kind is flag.

items.description: Present when the kind is list.

structured.description:
Present when the kind is structured: a JSON document, carried as
text.

A structured value is an object, or a list of them, and this schema
language offers no type for one — there is no Any, and a discriminated
union over the concrete types does not compile under this repository's
configuration. Carrying the JSON is what lets the value survive
intact; a renderer parses it and emits it as real structure, and a
consumer parses the string.

text.description: Present when the kind is text.

FlagAuthRow.description: An authorization row whose resolved value is yes or no.

Invocation.description: One step of the plan a command ran, as the audit line for it.

command.description:
The resolved command, quoted so it can be pasted into a shell.
Empty when the step did not run.

dir.description: The working directory it ran in. Empty means the caller's own.

duration_ms.description:
How long the invocation took, in whole milliseconds.

A count rather than a formatted duration: a field whose meaning depends
on the locale of the process that produced it is one this contract
forbids.

error.description:
Why the step failed, when it did: the process could not be started,
its decoder refused the result, or an argument could not be resolved.
A non-zero exit alone is not an error. Empty when there was none.

exit_status.description:
The status the finished process reported. Meaningful only when the
step ran; -1 when the process was terminated by a signal.

reason.description: Why a refused or skipped step did not run. Empty otherwise.

stderr_digest.description:
A digest of the whole standard error stream, separately, because the
streams are separate.

stdout_digest.description: A digest of the whole standard output stream, as sha256:<hex>.

step.description: The step's name within its plan.

PreFlightKeys.description:
Keys the run's pre-flight establishes.

Every key here is optional on the wire: the manifest is a partial record
that grows as a run proceeds, and a key's absence before its stage is a
legitimate state rather than a defect. What this struct asserts is the
stage at which each key becomes required, which is the fact validation
reads.

RunEffort.description:
How much reasoning effort the harness was set to for this run.

A harness that exposes no such setting records it as unrecorded rather
than leaving the key absent, so a reader can tell "not offered" from
"not yet written".

RunManifest.description:
The run manifest: the JSON object in a run epic's tracker metadata,
and the run's only durable record.

This is the whole declared key set. A key outside it is refused rather
than stored, and a value whose type is not its key's declared type is
refused, which is what the closed shape above expresses.

The stage at which a key becomes required is the first struct in the
chain that declares it — PreFlightKeys, then ScopeKeys, PlanKeys,
DispatchKeys, RetroKeys — so a key's name, its type and its stage all
come from one declaration.

trailers.description:
The commit trailers the run resolved.

Declared here rather than in a stage struct, and that placement is what
says it is never required: a run that resolved no trailer convention
legitimately carries none at every stage, so an absent value means that
rather than "not yet written". A key whose absence is always legitimate
has no stage, and having no stage is expressed by having no stage
struct.

RunStage.description:
The stages of a run, in the order a run reaches them.

A manifest key becomes required at the stage whose key struct declares it,
and the value here names that stage. The correspondence is structural:
the struct declaring a key IS the statement of its stage, so a key cannot
be given a type in one place and a stage in another.

StandingAuth.description:
The authorization gate's rows, each with its resolved value and where
that value came from.

Named fields rather than a map, because the rows are a fixed set and each
one's value has a fixed type: a map would have to carry a value of mixed
type, and there is no such thing in a closed schema. This is also what
lets the wire form stay exactly what the skills write today.
